title: Exam-Day Execution
summary: Executing a time plan in the hall: the on-screen test interface, the three-pass method with a worked plan for a 100-question prelims, a personal walk-away limit, choosing question order, and steadying yourself when a section goes wrong. Builds on Sectional Time Management. Guidance only.
learningObjectives: Navigate the computer-based test interface without wasting time on it.
Apply a three-pass sweep to a section and to the paper.
Use a fixed walk-away limit for a single question or set.
Choose question order by strength and recover from a shaky start.

blocks.title: This is the execution layer
blocks.markdown:
A separate topic covers the arithmetic of time - turning the clock into a per-question budget and running a section in rounds. This topic assumes that budget is set and deals with **executing it in the hall**: the software in front of you, the order you take questions in, and staying steady when a section does not go to plan.

Execution is a rehearsed skill. The interface, the pass pattern and the walk-away habit should all be automatic before exam day, practised in every full mock.

blocks.title: Know the interface cold
blocks.markdown:
The test is computer-based. Time lost fighting the software is time lost, so learn it on the **official practice interface** before the exam:

- **Question palette:** the grid of numbers, colour-coded for not visited, unanswered, answered, and marked for review. A glance tells you what is left.
- **Save and Next:** an answer is not recorded until you save it. Build the habit so you never leave a chosen answer unsaved.
- **Mark for Review:** flags a question to come back to. Use it for anything you did not answer with confidence; it is your pass-two list.
- **Section timer:** in the main stage each section has its own clock and you cannot carry spare time forward or borrow from the next. Watch the section timer, not just the total.

Do not change language, font size or other settings during the exam beyond a quick check at the start.

blocks.title: Worked example: three passes over a 100-question prelims
blocks.markdown:
Take a preliminary paper of 100 questions in 60 minutes, with English 30, reasoning 35 and quantitative aptitude 35, on a single overall clock.

**Pass 1 - about 40 minutes.** Go through all three sections in your preferred order. Answer only what you can do comfortably inside its budget. The moment a question resists, mark it for review and move on. Aim to clear roughly 60 to 70 confident attempts here.

**Pass 2 - about 15 minutes.** Return to the marked questions. Now you know which are worth the time. Solve the tractable ones; leave the rest marked.

**Pass 3 - about 5 minutes.** Scan the palette for anything unsaved. Recheck flagged answers you reasoned out. Take only the guesses that the rules favour - at least two options eliminated.

The split between sections inside pass 1 still follows your per-section budget; the three passes sit on top of that, not instead of it.

blocks.title: A fixed walk-away limit
blocks.markdown:
Set a hard limit for a single question - many candidates use about **45 seconds** for a standalone question, a little more for the first question of a data set - and obey it without negotiation.

When the limit hits and there is no clear path to the answer, mark for review and leave. A stuck question you refuse to release typically costs you three or four easy questions elsewhere. The limit protects those easy marks.

blocks.title: Choosing what to attempt first
blocks.markdown:
- **Within a section, start with your strongest question types**, not question one. In reasoning that may be the short puzzles and inequalities before the long arrangements; in quantitative aptitude, the direct calculations before the heavy data sets.
- **Scan a data-interpretation or puzzle set before committing.** Read the set, judge its difficulty, and either commit to the whole set or skip it - do not solve half and abandon it.
- **Take the section you are most confident in first** if the order is yours to choose on a single clock. A strong opening section settles the nerves and banks marks early.
- **Leave the reading-comprehension passage's global questions for last** within English; do the vocabulary and error items first.

blocks.title: When a section goes wrong
blocks.markdown:
- **Blanking on the first few questions is common.** Skip forward; an easier question resets your rhythm. Come back on pass two.
- **If panic rises,** stop for two slow breaths - in for four counts, out for four. Ten seconds spent here is cheaper than five minutes of scattered marking.
- **Do not chase a section that is going badly** by attempting more. Hold your accuracy, take the sure marks, and rely on the other sections and the overall total.
- **Final two minutes of a section:** save every chosen answer, take rule-favoured guesses on eliminated questions, and stop. Do not blind-fill a block of unread questions.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.markdown:
- **Sinking five minutes into one hard set** out of stubbornness - the classic sunk-cost error.
- **Watching only the master clock** in the main stage and overrunning a section timer.
- **Choosing an answer but not saving it,** so it never counts.
- **Not using Mark for Review,** then hunting through the paper for the questions you meant to revisit.
- **Changing a saved answer on a hunch** with no fresh reason - first instincts on a reasoned question are usually right.
- **Panic-filling the last thirty seconds** with blind guesses at a one-fourth penalty.

blocks.title: Quick revision
blocks.markdown:
- This topic executes a time plan; the per-question budget comes from Sectional Time Management.
- Learn the interface on the official mock: question palette, Save and Next, Mark for Review, and the per-section timer you cannot carry forward.
- Run three passes: pass 1 confident attempts only (about 40 of 60 minutes on a 100-question prelims), pass 2 the marked questions, pass 3 unsaved answers and rule-favoured guesses.
- Keep a fixed walk-away limit (around 45 seconds for a standalone question) and obey it.
- Start each section with your strongest question types; scan a set before committing; do the whole set or skip it.
- Recover from a bad start by skipping forward and holding accuracy; never chase a weak section with more attempts or blind-fill at the end.

blocks.title: Practice
blocks.markdown:
Pick the best response and give a one-line reason.

1. You are 90 seconds into a single reasoning question with no clear path. What do you do?
2. In the main stage you have 6 minutes left overall but this section's timer shows 40 seconds. Which clock governs?
3. You solved three of the five questions in a data set and it is fighting you. Continue or move on?
4. You blank on the first four questions of quantitative aptitude. Best move?
5. On pass two you reread a saved answer and feel unsure, but have no new reasoning. Change it?
6. Thirty seconds left in the section, eight questions untouched. Blind-fill them?

**Answers.** 1 Mark for review and leave - you are past a sensible walk-away limit and it is costing easier marks. 2 The section timer - in the main stage you cannot use the spare overall time here. 3 Move on - commit to a whole set or leave it; half-solving wastes the reading. 4 Skip forward to an easier question to reset rhythm, return on pass two. 5 No - without fresh reasoning, keep the first reasoned answer. 6 No - blind-fill averages to zero at a one-fourth penalty and only adds variance; save what you have and stop.

flashcards.front: What are the three passes over an objective paper?
flashcards.back: Pass 1: sweep every section, answer only confident questions, mark the rest. Pass 2: return to the marked questions. Pass 3: save any unsaved answers and take rule-favoured guesses.

flashcards.front: Why keep a fixed walk-away limit of about 45 seconds per standalone question?
flashcards.back: A question you refuse to release typically costs three or four easy questions elsewhere. The limit protects those marks.
flashcards.explanation: Mark for review at the limit and move on, no negotiation.

flashcards.front: In the test interface, when is your chosen answer actually recorded?
flashcards.back: Only when you save it (Save and Next). An option clicked but not saved does not count.
flashcards.explanation: Build the save habit so it is automatic.

flashcards.front: In the main stage, which clock do you watch - the overall timer or the section timer?
flashcards.back: The section timer. Each section has its own clock and spare time cannot be carried forward or borrowed from the next.
flashcards.explanation: Overrunning a section timer is a common avoidable loss.

flashcards.front: Where should you start within a section?
flashcards.back: With your strongest question types, not with question one. Bank the sure marks first, then spend the remaining time on the harder items.
flashcards.explanation: Questions need not be attempted in serial order.

flashcards.front: You have solved two of five questions in a puzzle set and it is fighting you. What now?
flashcards.back: Move on. Commit to a whole set or skip it; half-solving spends the reading time for a fraction of the marks.
flashcards.explanation: Scan a set and judge its difficulty before committing.

flashcards.front: A section is going badly. Do you attempt more questions to make it up?
flashcards.back: No. Hold your accuracy, take the sure marks, and rely on the other sections and the overall total. Chasing a weak section scatters errors.
flashcards.explanation: Skip forward past a blank spot; breathe; come back on pass two.
